note: Stories are narrative editions of completed game turns, not executable save files. The canonical game state remains in data/taluma.json.

stories.title: The Space Between Hearths
stories.deck: A grown founding child chooses an independent hearth, Taluma audits seasonal trade, and the northern rocks remain beyond safe knowledge.

sections.heading: I. A hearth of one's own
paragraphs: The first request came from Nes, a young adult who had been a child when Taluma's first families gathered beside the lagoon. Nes had grown into a careful maker of basket frames but still shared a family hearth. Now the work crowded the household's sleeping space, and Nes asked Seli whether a person could live separately without first finding a spouse.

Seli brought the question to the Hall of Many Hands instead of treating it as a marriage problem. Maro's voluntary census had found nineteen unpartnered adults, and nine founding-era children who were now grown but still shared their original family hearths. Neither number revealed what anyone wanted. Some preferred their extended households. Others supported relatives who needed care. None owed Taluma a wedding or a move.

Nes and a relative inspected an unused room already counted among Taluma's 118 housing places. The repairs used ordinary unearmarked reeds and lashings, not the construction kit spent on the five-place home. The council recorded a separate cooking hearth only after Nes requested it and the space passed Seli's inspection. Nes still visited the family table. Another grown adult asked for information about leaving and chose to stay.

At the public readback, Seli reported twenty-nine hearth households, one more than before. Eight of the original nine grown founding children still shared family homes. The nineteen unpartnered adults remained nineteen, including sixteen working-age adults and three elders. Population was still 112, with six unoccupied housing places. 'You haven't left us,' Nes's relative said. 'No,' Nes answered. 'I just have a door I can close.'

sections.heading: II. What survives the crossing
paragraphs: Under Taluma's market awning, Aret made an apprentice set the travel costs beside the food tally. Dava prepared one card for what Taluma sent, another for what came back, and a third for the crew time, fuel and repairs spent moving it. Iset had demanded the third card after hearing too many exchanges described as if the boats rowed themselves.

A Shellbend household and a Reedmouth household each accepted another invitation. A Crescent Shoal craft visitor independently offered prepared poles and reeds. The buyer-selected food samples were opened in front of both parties. One lot failed its center-dryness check and was withdrawn, with the loss entered beside ordinary spoilage rather than hidden inside the sales numbers.

Across two separately consented exchanges, twelve settlement-days of Taluman food went out and five days of food came back. Two wood poles and three reed bundles entered the materials register. Three food-days were rejected or spoiled across the turn. On another modest comparison, fourteen of sixteen raised-screen lots remained sound at inspection, compared with twelve of sixteen on the older covered shelves. Aret refused to convert those small tests into promises of storm-proof storage.

The extra goods were useful. So were a visitor's better packing method and the fact that returning buyers felt free to reject a doubtful packet. But Nemi would not call a net loss of seven food-days a food profit. Smoke fuel, coastal crew labor, household hospitality and basket repairs had all cost something. When a recorder suggested writing 'reliable network' next to the three shore names, Maro shook his head. Each household could decline its next invitation. Taluma was gaining trust, not signing away its stores. The provisional 180-day food floor remained intact.

sections.heading: III. A line that stays outside the rocks
paragraphs: Ilan waited at Upper Path while Oru and Tesh carried a fresh question to Renka. The previous approved meeting created no continuing right to use her people's tracks. Renka chose one sheltered bench on gentle Upper Windgrass ground and agreed to meet there. Kelan brought a carrying frame and spare cord, not quarrying tools or gear for the forbidden loose-stone descent.

A wet quick-release strap shifted in one early turn, tipping an empty practice basket into the grass. Renka stopped the work. Her companion demonstrated how a tired carrier could lower the load before releasing the shoulder band, instead of trusting a knot to behave under strain. Ten of twelve later controlled carries stayed secure; two shifted during turns. Leni credited Kelan and both Ridge Hearth teachers. There was no steep-ground qualification, no copying of private trail signs, and no standing permission to return.

Back at the Hall, Letha spread the existing Northreach hide atlas before Keshu. Six prior soundings marked known safe offshore water through two tidal states. They did not tell anyone what lay behind the narrow rock notch. Keshu traced the line where a cross-current had persisted even when the surface looked deceptively calm. Letha proposed repeating flood and ebb readings from a carefully chosen offshore observation station, never inside the notch, with explicit retreat limits and a fresh Ternhook stopping invitation.

They tested the proposed sounding marks in Taluma's sheltered inlet first. A wet rope made some marks hard to distinguish. The learners widened their spacing and checked them again. Neither Reedwing nor Tidefin sailed toward Northreach this turn. The boats remained available for ordinary permitted travel. A blank remained beyond the rocks on the atlas, where a blank belonged.

At the season's final gathering, Nes sat near relatives from the old hearth. Taluma had made room for an independent life without requiring a marriage, learned to count the costs of trade without losing its appetite for exchange, and refused to mistake a safer plan for a safe passage. Esha listened to the report and asked the apprentice recorder to read every limitation aloud.

stories.title: The Hearths We Share
stories.deck: A newly counted generation, an honest market, a host-chosen meeting and a northern tide that still refuses passage.

sections.heading: The hearth where they belong
paragraphs: Hesa had lived at Taluma for a season before he admitted what worried him. His fishing-net repairs were welcome, Ruva had a place at the reed workshop, and Naro had already learned the quickest route to the Hall of Many Hands. But Hesa's sister was still in Reedmouth, and he had missed a family gathering there.

Seli suggested a visit rather than another speech about belonging. On the next permitted coastal journey, Hesa returned to Reedmouth with a repair sample, stayed with his relatives and came back at his own chosen time. Ruva joined Maren in testing basket linings against damp fish stores. Naro helped Seli count shells in a voluntary reading lesson and was not assigned adult work. Nothing required the family to cut ties with the inlet they had left.

The episode led Seli to a question the council had never properly counted. Taluma knew it had sixty-three working-age adults, forty-two children and seven elders. It did not know exactly how many adults lived without a partner, or how many of the children who had grown up during Taluma's seventeen years still lived at their original family hearths.

Maro proposed a household roll. Twenty-eight households gave voluntary aggregate answers with private checking, and he kept names off the public tally. There were nineteen unpartnered adults among seventy adult and elder residents, including sixteen of the sixty-three working-age adults and three elders. Nine people who had been children in Taluma's founding households were now working-age adults and still shared their family hearths. These two groups could overlap. The count said nothing about who wished to marry or leave home.

One young adult asked whether sharing a hearth made them a burden. Seli answered, "Only if we stop asking who carries the work." Taluma's 118 housing places still had six vacancies. No new birth, death, immigration or relocation was recorded.

sections.heading: A market that can say no
paragraphs: The next invited trade gathering opened with Dava's inspection table placed where visitors could reach it. Aret had changed the labels again. Each sound packet bore the preparation date, the two Taluman witnesses, and an empty place for a buyer's mark. A guest could choose and open a sample or refuse the lot entirely.

A Shellbend buyer found one packet that did not meet the agreed dry-center test. Aret pulled the entire questioned lot from the offer. A Reedmouth visitor then brought a different, honestly described lot of household provisions, while a consenting Windcut craft visitor demonstrated a narrower replaceable basket binding. No visitor was treated as representing every household on their shore.

Taluma traded twelve settlement-days of inspected food and accepted four days of incoming food. One wood pole and two reed bundles entered the nonfood ledger, and the demonstration was entered as knowledge rather than fictional profit. Three settlement-days of unsound or spoiled stores were discarded. Aret's apprentice noticed the public figures made the market appear less successful than the older stories about abundance.
"Good," Iset said when the totals were read. "Now someone who isn't here can tell what actually happened."

The council retained the 180-day provisional food floor and refused a request for assured seasonal quantities. Windcut's visitor had offered a trial design, not a standing commercial alliance. Repeatable quality, independent rejection and honest cost records were worth more than promising goods Taluma could not yet preserve reliably.

sections.heading: The sea and the other shore
paragraphs: Oru and Tesh took Ilan's question to Renka. The old two-window protocol had expired with its last meeting, and Taluma sent neither a traveling party nor a marker without a new answer. Renka permitted one craft gathering on an upper Windgrass shelter bench chosen by her household, not the dangerous descent. She asked in return whether one of her learners might someday visit Taluma's public workshop. Ilan offered an invitation but left the decision with the learner.

Kelan brought the lower-load carrying frame; Renka's companion tested the quick release of its shoulder band. Seven of eight controlled, gentle-ground trials stayed secure. In the eighth, the released frame tilted toward the carrier's ankle. Renka stopped the lesson and ordered the strap moved. Nobody claimed steep-path safety. They agreed that any additional visit would require another independent invitation. Taluma made no permanent route and copied no private signs.

A few weeks later, Keshu confirmed one narrower daylight window of comparatively calm outer water. A Ternhook household separately granted Reedwing a single sheltered stopping visit. Letha carried a measured sounding line and extra provisions north. From previously observed safe water she made six soundings over two tidal states. Beneath the apparently open notch she saw a transverse current persist, even when the sea surface looked smooth. The crew turned back without crossing it.

At Taluma, Maro marked six new offshore observations on the existing hide atlas. He did not draw the unvisited water behind the rocks. It would be easy, he said, for a child learning the records to mistake a confident line for a place someone had walked.

Hesa had returned from Reedmouth before the boats came home. At the evening reading he stood beside Ruva and Naro, listening while Maro named both discoveries and limits. Taluma had learned how many of its grown children still lived with family, how to lose an uncertain sale without losing a neighbor, and why an open-looking coast might remain impassable. None of these required another household to surrender its choices.

stories.title: The Doors We May Open
stories.deck: One Reedmouth family chooses Taluma. A market learns the difference between trade and profit, Renka welcomes a final seasonal visit, and a dangerous northern passage remains unopened.

sections.heading: The price of belonging
paragraphs: The Reedmouth family did not arrive with a procession. They came first as guests, in a borrowed boat, with two small bundles and a question. Hesa repaired fishing nets; Ruva worked reeds into basket linings, and their child Naro had spent most of the crossing staring toward Taluma’s drying racks. None had asked to be enrolled as citizens when they visited the season before. They had wanted to know whether they could choose a new home and still leave if it proved wrong.

Seli showed them the empty five-place house, then showed them the less attractive parts of living in Taluma: the shared care roster, communal repairs, the open council hearings and the expectation that disputes could be spoken aloud. Ruva asked whether she would be permitted to bring her own method of lining fish baskets. “If it works,” Aret answered, “we will measure it. If it fails, we will measure that too.”

On their second visit, Iset asked Hesa what he would miss about Reedmouth. “My sister,” he replied. “And the inlet before the rain.” No one promised an easy answer to either problem. Taluma offered voluntary work, safe water, space and a path back to their relations. The household returned home to discuss the move without an escort waiting at their door.

On Day 265 the three returned with their own gear and accepted residence. Maro entered two adults and one child in the census. Seli inspected the home once more before they crossed its threshold. Taluma had 112 residents, twenty-eight household hearths, and six available housing places. The change was not a decree or a rush of settlers. One family had decided to stay.

sections.heading: What a market actually earns
paragraphs: Nemi’s fourth round of modest seasonal trading began with a ledger that looked less triumphant than the older tally boards. Aret and Dava required that a buyer choose a packet to open, and that each inspected batch carry two independent witnesses. One lot of cured fish passed Taluma’s own check but failed a buyer’s examination when its center proved too damp. The entire questionable batch was withdrawn. Its loss was entered with other rejected stock, not charged to the visitor.

Shellbend and Reedmouth buyers accepted separate exchanges. A Crescent visitor observed a packaging demonstration and offered a method for keeping reed covers away from the wet hull of a boat; Taluma could try it, but no new contract followed. One other household chose not to trade. The market sent fourteen settlement-days of inspected food outward and brought five days of other provisions back, together with one prepared pole and two reed bundles counted outside the food ledger.

“We gave more food than we received,” Iset said when Maro read back the tally. Nemi agreed. He listed what could not be measured as food: a better wrapping demonstration, an additional household willing to inspect Taluma’s goods, and knowledge of what buyers refused. He would not enter those things as fictitious food-days of profit. The apprentices would follow later invitations and rejected lots before the council called this a reliable regional network.

The raised and screened shelves continued to give better small-batch results, but not without repairs. Four settlement-days of spoiled or rejected food were recorded for the period. The council kept its provisional 180-day reserve floor, even as the extra mouths in the new house made each settlement-day a larger demand.

sections.heading: The second invitation and the water that waited
paragraphs: Ilan waited at Upper Path while the adult route host Oru and Tesh carried Taluma’s request to Renka. Only one potential seasonal meeting remained under their revocable arrangement. Renka agreed, but moved the gathering from the earlier shelf to a different safe part of the established Upper Windgrass meeting ground. The visitors accepted her choice rather than asking why the old place was unavailable.

Kelan brought a detachable carrying strap based on Renka’s loading advice. Renka’s companion adjusted the shoulder support; Leni watched the knots and wrote down each contribution. In ten short load trials on gently damp ground, eight held steady. Two shifted when a tired carrier turned. Renka ended the demonstration rather than extending the tests toward the closed loose-stone descent.

She did, however, show them how to unload safely without letting a heavy basket drag the wearer sideways. Leni credited the host teachers by name and left their private trail marks out of the archive. The second seasonal meeting window was now used. Future visits would require a new, independently negotiated invitation, not an automatic renewal of the old protocol.

At the Hall, Letha brought the northern hide atlas to the council. She had drafted a more systematic offshore survey: repeat soundings from previously safe water, compare flood and ebb on separate days, carry food for a return journey and obtain a new Ternhook stop before departure. Keshu had not confirmed safer outer tides, and no new host permission had arrived. Reedwing and Tidefin remained ready for ordinary work, but no boat sailed toward the dangerous notch.

Esha listened as Maro read the decision alongside the welcome of Hesa, Ruva and Naro. A new family had crossed a threshold freely. Renka had opened a meeting and then closed it on her terms. A hidden passage remained hidden. Taluma had grown, but it was learning that there were different kinds of doors, and no honor in forcing the ones that belonged to someone else.

stories.title: The Packet, the Path and the Passage
stories.deck: A doubtful food lot is withdrawn, Renka hosts the first revocable seasonal craft meeting, and a northern passage remains unentered.

sections.heading: The packet set aside
paragraphs: The third trading gathering began with an argument before a single basket changed hands. Aret had arranged Taluma’s smoked fish under a clean awning, each packet bearing the lot mark of the preparer and a second witness. A Reedmouth buyer selected one from the center of a group rather than accepting the packet placed nearest the front. The cut surface was sound, but a corner felt damp. Aret withdrew the entire lot for reinspection.

“Then why give it a mark at all?” asked one of the younger apprentices. Dava took the tablet from him and drew a line through the quantity promised for sale. “Because we can find the doubtful ones before a neighbor eats them.” The buyer returned the following morning, inspected a different lot, and accepted it without demanding that the first be concealed.

Nemi had invited willing Shellbend and Reedmouth households individually. A Crescent Shoal visitor watched a demonstration but made no purchase or future promise; the Ternhook party declined the crossing during rough weather. Nobody was counted as having agreed merely because Taluma offered a place. Across the accepted visits, twelve settlement-days of inspected provisions left Taluma and five came back in other foods. Some trade returned wood and reeds, entered separately from food. Four settlement-days of local stores failed inspection, including the withdrawn market lot.

The raised-screen racks again performed better in a small comparative check: twenty-three of twenty-six lots stayed sound at their scheduled opening, compared with twenty of twenty-six from older covered shelves. Aret kept the result on the Hall wall without a claim that the method could guarantee food through a whole season. Iset asked for transport labor and spoiled batches to appear beside sales figures. Maro recorded the objection and the corrected net movement in the public hearing.

sections.heading: The meeting that could end
paragraphs: At Upper Path, Ilan waited while Oru and Tesh carried a request toward Renka’s people. The two-season meeting arrangement promised only a way of asking, and this was its first actual test. Renka’s household chose the sheltered upper Windgrass shelf, the number of visitors and a clear morning for a supervised craft exchange. No one used private path signs, and the loose-stone descent remained closed.

Kelan brought two versions of the low-hung carrying frame. Renka’s companion tightened the broad shoulder band while Kelan replaced the outer grip sleeve. With stone baskets on gentle, damp ground, fourteen of sixteen short passes held. One load sagged when the carrier stopped abruptly; another twisted during a turn. Renka halted the trial, loosened the strap and demonstrated why a tired carrier needed a way to lower the load without being dragged sideways.

Leni wrote the teaching credit with three names: Kelan, Renka and Renka’s companion. She did not invent a new Shore Words translation for the host’s gestures. The participants exchanged small, inspected provisions and two trial cordage coils, counted within Taluma’s hospitality and material ledgers. They made no durable road and no claim that the method was safe on steep slopes.

When Ilan asked whether the next seasonal gathering could be placed on the same shelf, Renka shook her head. She pointed toward the neighboring families’ resting ground, then back to Oru. Next time they would ask again; the hosts might choose somewhere else, or decline altogether. One of the two possible seasonal meeting windows had now been used. The second was still only an opportunity to request permission.

sections.heading: Nine places and a narrow tide
paragraphs: Seli inspected the new five-place house with Kiva, Ralen and an older learner who had helped weave its panels. After hard rain, a low reed edge showed signs of loosening. The repair crew reset it with materials from ordinary stores, not from the old home kit that had already been spent. The water and care rosters could serve the house if it filled, but no resident had yet moved in.

A visiting Reedmouth household asked what living in Taluma would require. Seli showed them the empty dwelling, the shared care rota and the ordinary expectations of a household joining the settlement. She did not assign them a bed or enter their names on the census. They returned home to discuss the decision among themselves. For now Taluma remained 109 residents with nine available places, and the council maintained the home for future voluntary use.

The northern question returned when Keshu brought word of a short, comparatively calm daylight interval and a Ternhook household independently welcomed one sheltered stop. Letha took Reedwing with a small crew, Keshu piloting the known approach. They watched the outer rocks from a safe position through flood and ebb, using the sounding line only within waters already judged suitable for the boat.

From one angle the northern notch seemed to divide into two openings. As the ebb strengthened, a cross-current swept along the nearer lip and exposed stones beneath what had looked like smooth water. Letha refused the passage and returned with two witnessed tide observations. Maro added the divided appearance to the hide atlas as an offshore observation, not a mapped channel. No new landing, territorial claim or safe crossing had been established.

That evening Esha listened as the apprentices read back three separate marks: a packet withdrawn rather than sold, a meeting that could be declined, and a passage left unentered. None sounded grand. They were, however, the kind of decisions Taluma’s children could inherit without inheriting anyone else’s risk.

stories.title: The House With Empty Places
stories.deck: Taluma tests a seasonal food market, spends its long-protected house kit, and learns that lasting friendship begins with the right to decline.

sections.heading: I. The baskets at the door
paragraphs: The first visitor to question Taluma’s new seasonal food market was not a stranger. It was Iset, watching Aret place three inspected fish packets beneath the Hall’s eastern awning. “If one packet fails,” she asked, “whose mark is the buyer meant to trust?”

Aret did not answer with another mark. She invited the Shellbend and Reedmouth guests to choose their own sample from each offered lot. When one selected packet proved damp at its center, she removed the whole suspect batch from sale. Dava recorded the rejection beside the names of the people who had checked it. The visiting fisher watched the correction, then agreed to inspect a different lot.

Nemi had wanted a market that might return at the change of each season. What he obtained was two successful, separately invited gatherings, with no guaranteed third. A Shellbend household took cured fish; Reedmouth traders brought different edible stores and practical wrapping materials. Fourteen settlement-days of inspected Taluman food went outward and five days of other provisions came in. A few poles and reeds received in barter were entered under materials, not food. The rejected packets counted against Taluma’s own spoilage.

An apprentice asked whether the traders could simply take the same amount next season. “Not until they agree to come,” Maro said. “And not until we know the food is fit to leave.” Aret’s new comparisons were encouraging: eleven of twelve carefully raised-and-screened trial lots remained sound at inspection, against nine of twelve older covered lots. No one called that a guarantee through a long voyage, and the public tally said so.

sections.heading: II. The roof before the family
paragraphs: On a dry morning, Seli led several households to a small prepared plot within Taluma’s existing settlement. The village had only four unoccupied housing places. The five-person home kit had been kept apart in the material ledger for years: four poles, seven reed bundles, one stone load and one cordage coil. Today, for the first time, its witnesses authorized those materials to be used rather than merely guarded.

Hadan and the repair crew raised the framework while volunteers prepared reed panels and a sheltered cooking approach. Nobody was ordered away from caregiving or from essential water and food work. When a gust lifted one roof edge, Seli insisted on another fastening before anyone moved inside. The correction delayed completion by several days and used part of the ordinary repair allotment.

Dava counted the house twice: once as a structure and once as a responsibility. There would be ongoing roof inspections, fuel needs and space for people who had not yet arrived. Esha agreed that an empty house was not evidence of a promised migration. Taluma had built room for five more residents, but had not compelled a marriage, invited a large group, or claimed any new shore.

At the second inspection, rain ran away from the threshold. The new home passed its practical checks, bringing capacity from 113 to 118 places. All 109 residents remained in their existing households. Nine places stood open, including the newly prepared home. The kit’s materials were now spent and recorded as construction, not still described as an untouched reserve.

sections.heading: III. A meeting that can be declined
paragraphs: Ilan carried Taluma’s proposed seasonal gathering marks only as far as Upper Path. Oru and Tesh took the question to Renka’s household; no one followed them uninvited. When Renka chose to meet on the familiar Upper Windgrass shelf, Kelan brought a familiar frame and no new load to test on the dangerous descent.

Renka was interested in meeting again. She was less interested in strangers assuming the same route would always be theirs. She drew a short line in the damp ground, placed two pebbles for two possible seasons, and wiped away the line between them. Leni understood enough to ask for the terms to be repeated by demonstration.

The households present agreed to a modest arrangement: during each of the next two seasonal windows, Taluma might request one escorted craft meeting at a location chosen by the Ridge Hearth hosts. A separate meeting at Taluma’s Hall could be offered in return. Each actual visit required fresh assent from the relevant people, and either side could decline or cancel without penalty. No permanent path signs, unescorted access, exclusive trade or rights over another household’s land followed from the agreement.

Kelan showed the frame’s low-load support, now credited in the teaching record to him, Renka and her companion. A strap still pulled sideways when turned sharply, so Renka kept the demonstration on safe ground. The day ended not with a new road, but with a clear way to ask for the next meeting.

When the report reached the Hall, Iset asked whether the seasonal pebbles meant Taluma could go inland twice without waiting for a reply. Maro answered in the public record: “They mean we know how to ask. Nothing more.” Seven councillors remained at their seats, and the story of the agreement was read aloud with both its possibilities and its limits.

stories.title: The Names Beneath the Marks
stories.deck: A food mark must earn a stranger's trust. Renka shares credit for a safer load, and the northern voyage waits for the sea to agree.

sections.heading: I. A mark that means something
paragraphs: The first of the late-year storms pushed rain beneath the edges of Taluma’s newest drying screens. Aret found the damage before the fish beneath them turned. She had insisted that the apprentices inspect by touch and smell, not merely count the marks on the basket. This time, the marks gave her a place to begin: they named the batch, the preparation and the person who had last looked inside.

Dava and the six rotating learners brought their latest comparisons to Nemi. Of twenty-four small lots kept on the revised raised racks, twenty-one were sound at their scheduled inspection. Seventeen of twenty-four lots on the older covered shelves were sound. The improvement had appeared twice now, across different weather, though no one could yet promise how any particular parcel would endure an entire distant journey. Four settlement-days of food had been rejected across Taluma’s stores this turn, including wet-weather losses that kept the apprentices humble.

At the shore market, a Reedmouth visitor examined a packet and asked, through patient gestures, why Taluma’s witness marks should mean anything beyond its own walls. Dava opened a companion packet and showed how two different people checked the same batch. The visitor asked to select one at random. Aret let him. It was sound.
“That is what the mark must survive,” Dava said when he left. “Someone else looking.”

Separately invited visitors from Shellbend, Reedmouth and a Ternhook household accepted modest, inspected exchanges. Eighteen settlement-days of Taluman food went out, six days of different provisions returned, and two prepared poles and three reed bundles entered the material tally. Nobody purchased access, promised a monthly delivery or surrendered a fishing place. When one trader suggested that his household should have first claim on Taluma’s best smoked fish, Maro wrote it as an offer, not an agreement.

sections.heading: II. Whose hands made it?
paragraphs: Ilan returned inland only after Oru and Tesh secured another invitation from Renka’s people. Kelan brought a revised carrying frame: its load hung lower, with two separately tied gripping supports and a shoulder band shaped after Renka’s demonstration. The meeting stayed on the upper Windgrass shelf. The stone descent was still forbidden.

Twenty low, carefully weighted passages were attempted on gentle ground, with stops for inspection. Eighteen kept their loads secure. Twice the weight shifted when the carrier turned too quickly. Neither carrier was hurt, but Renka ended the test there. The result was sufficient for supervised work on Taluma’s familiar, level paths; it was not permission to haul through Ridge Hearth’s steep country.
Kelan wanted the new frame entered in the Taluman skills register. Leni, holding the witness board, hesitated. “As whose design?” she asked.

Kelan had changed the lashings. Renka had changed the loading. Her companion had shown the shoulder band. Without all three, the result would have been less secure. Ilan repeated each contribution slowly enough for the visitors to confirm it, and Leni recorded a jointly taught gentle-path method rather than a Taluman invention.

Renka nodded at that. She permitted a separate future request for another exchange, but no permanent trail markers, protected signs or passage rights. The participants took their borrowed examples home. Their knowledge could travel; their permission did not.

sections.heading: III. The choice not to go
paragraphs: At the next Hall hearing, Letha laid Reedwing’s sounding line beside the northern hide atlas. She wanted another observation of the dangerous notch beyond Northreach. The vessels were serviceable, the provisions ready, and the crew willing. But Keshu’s message from Crescent Shoal warned of unstable outer tides, and no fresh Ternhook stop had yet been confirmed.
An apprentice argued that all their past preparation would be wasted if they turned the boat back before leaving. Letha let him finish.
“A line with knots is not a promise that the sea will hold still,” she said.

The council postponed the outer voyage. Tidefin carried out ordinary coastal work inside known permissions, and the spare survey provisions remained in the counted stores. Maro left the tidal notch marked as observed from offshore, with the passage beyond it explicitly unknown. Nobody filled a blank on the atlas merely to make the season appear productive.

That evening Iset stood before the seven councillors and asked how the new trade marks would be challenged when a bad packet did slip through. The council adopted a small, reversible practice: a buyer could open a witnessed sample before acceptance, and a disputed lot would be withdrawn from the current exchange until inspected again. Taluma was not promising compensation it could not measure, nor imposing its rules on other shores. It was offering a reason to trust the next packet.

Esha looked over the tally boards. The village was still 109 people, and the seven seats were still filled. Their children were learning more than how to count stores or tie knots. They were learning how to admit another person might know something Taluma did not.

stories.title: The Measure of a Promise
stories.deck: Reliable food, a safer inland load, and a northern opening that may not be a passage. Taluma learns what trust costs.

sections.heading: The value of a promise
paragraphs: At the Hall of Many Hands, Nemi set a sound smoked-fish packet beside a spoiled one. From the outside they were nearly indistinguishable. Aret loosened the second binding and its damp center answered for them.
"Nobody trades with a basket's tally mark," Nemi said. "They trade with whoever put that mark there."

Dava and six rotating apprentices tracked comparable lots. Ten of twelve batches on improved raised shelves remained sound; on the older covered shelves, eight of twelve were sound. The difference mattered, but Aret would not claim a full season's proof. Wind-driven rain reached some screens and three settlement-days of damaged or questionable food were lost.

Shellbend households accepted an invited exchange. Reedmouth traders inspected dated packets. A Ternhook household received a trial lot at a permitted landing. Fifteen settlement-days of inspected food left Taluma; five days of other provisions returned alongside separately counted materials.
When a visitor asked about automatic monthly deliveries, Maro crossed the word "promised" from an apprentice's notes. "A second invitation is not owed because the first was pleasant."

sections.heading: Renka changes the question
paragraphs: Ilan waited at Upper Path while Oru and Tesh secured permission from Renka's household. Kelan brought a frame with a lower load point and two replaceable grips. Renka chose gentle wet ground for fourteen trials. Twelve loads stayed secure; two shifted. One carrier suffered a minor bruise, and the group stopped to inspect the assembly.
Renka adjusted the shoulder strap and showed how the load moved in a turn.
"You changed the knot," Ilan told Kelan, following her gestures. "She changed the load."

Later, Renka's companion visited Taluma to teach the combination at the Hall. Leni credited the host teachers and did not record private route signs. No permanent corridor or territorial right followed.

sections.heading: The opening in the northern rocks
paragraphs: Letha, Rela and Keshu took Reedwing north, using an approved Ternhook stopping place. Beyond Northreach Estuary the crew approached the dark ridge that had haunted earlier voyages.

With a marked sounding line and sufficient provisions to observe a tide cycle, Letha saw a narrow opening between outer rocks. During flood tide, water seemed to continue farther inland. Keshu would not call it a channel.
When the tide reversed, white water boiled over stones that had been hidden. Letha ordered Reedwing away.
Back at Taluma, Maro put two separate marks on the hide atlas: one for the observed notch and another for an unverified possible passage. Nobody landed or claimed the place.

sections.heading: The public record
paragraphs: Iset questioned the cost of promising deliveries before Taluma knew what the exchanges truly returned. Maro read the food and boat costs aloud. The council agreed each future delivery required fresh consent, verified goods and a separate decision.
Esha listened. All seven councillors still served, but the constitution was no longer an abstraction. People were challenging decisions and improving policy without destabilizing the community.
Nila slept through the argument on Seli's lap. Taluma had survived scarcity; now it was learning the responsibilities of abundance.

stories.title: The Price of Plenty
stories.deck: Taluma's storage apprentices learn to distrust their own marks, Renka refuses unsafe shortcuts, and a child is born.

sections.heading: A different kind of harvest
paragraphs: At Taluma's oldest drying house, Aret cut the tie on a basket marked three times and counted twice. The fish near the rim was sound; the center had become damp.
"If the mark only means somebody looked at it," Dava said, "we haven't learned anything."

Aret and six rotating apprentices separated small lots between tightly covered shelves and raised cross-ventilated racks. Each received preparation and inspection marks. The ventilated lots stayed drier, but an open screen admitted insects until Seli insisted on a narrower weave. Four settlement-days of questionable stores were rejected in the turn.

Fourteen settlement-days of inspected food left Taluma through modest exchanges and gifts. Five days came back as other preserved provisions, alongside distinct craft materials. When a trader suggested a much larger shipment, Nemi refused to treat tomorrow's reserves as today's bargaining chips.
"Next year's hungry people do not get a vote in today's bargain," he said.

sections.heading: Renka's lesson
paragraphs: At Upper Windgrass, Ilan and Kelan met Renka through Oru and Tesh, after the host households invited them. The dangerous descent remained closed.

Kelan widened the shoulder support on his frame and revised its gripping sleeve. Ten of twelve wet-ground trials succeeded on level terrain. Two loads shifted on sharp turns. Renka stopped the experiment before anyone tried the treacherous slope.
The visitors shared inspected food and packing methods while Renka's people demonstrated a different weight distribution. A future invitation was offered but no permanent passage was granted.

sections.heading: The public record and a new life
paragraphs: Iset challenged a proposed food shipment for being discussed while many fishers were at sea. The council held a second hearing and reduced the shipment to the fourteen settlement-days in the accounts.

Reedwing also completed a provisioned northern reconnaissance using an approved stopping place. Beyond Northreach, the crew saw broken rock and difficult shoals. They turned back instead of attempting an uncertain passage.
On Day 278, Kiva gave birth to Nila. Ralen cared for the household while their older child Aven waited with a folded reed mat. The birth brought Taluma to 109 residents, with no deaths or migration.
Esha listened as the next council reading announced the number. One hundred and nine.

stories.title: The Measure of Enough
stories.deck: Taluma stops mistaking a full storehouse for prosperity, tests Renka's improved frames, and makes accountability practical.

sections.heading: The abundance problem
paragraphs: By the time warm winds crossed Taluma's drying racks, Nemi had learned that a large store could demand as much judgment as an empty one.

Dava and six rotating apprentices inspected dated baskets. Some bundles remained sound enough to travel. Others entered ordinary meals promptly. Four settlement-days of spoiled or damaged stock were discarded. Aret experimented with raised, cross-ventilated store platforms. Two early lids trapped moisture and had to be dismantled.

At a public hearing, Iset challenged the idea that all incoming food trade was pure profit. If Taluma sent fifteen days of food and received eight days of other food, it had not gained seven days. Maro corrected the accounts to record outgoing and incoming goods separately.

The council adopted a durable food policy: protect a provisional 180 settlement-day floor, rotate inspected stores, support family recovery and nutrition, and commit only verified surplus to voluntary exchanges and voyages.
The important measure was now usable food, not just a large number.

sections.heading: Renka changes the load
paragraphs: Ilan and Kelan reached Upper Windgrass only after Oru and Tesh obtained permission. Renka's household chose the meeting place and excluded the dangerous loose-stone descent.

Kelan tested a lower load point with a replaceable gripping sleeve. Renka insisted on stone-filled baskets rather than fragile cargo or people. Seven of eight wet-ground trials held; one shifted during a turn. The result was promising, not proof that the design was safe for steep hauling.

Renka's companion demonstrated a woven shoulder support that spread pressure. Leni recorded the movements, leaving private trail symbols off the teaching tablets. The visitors offered inspected food and two cordage coils in an openly counted exchange.
"A path isn't yours because you know where it goes," Kelan told the apprentices later.

sections.heading: The work of a constitution
paragraphs: Iset challenged a council proposal discussed in the morning while fishers and caregivers could not attend. Maro recorded her objection. At a second hearing, costs became clearer and the council limited the shipment to the amount already accounted for.
Seven councillors still occupied seven seats. Nobody had died, resigned or inherited a position. The new constitution was working through ordinary criticism and corrected numbers.

Meanwhile, Windcut's fishers tried further sample lashings on their own removable frame. A sleeved binding resisted slipping but showed abrasion; another loosened after being retied with wet hands. Vessa refused commercial export until a longer test justified it.

stories.title: The Choice of Seven
stories.deck: The constitution is completed, food abundance gets a serious audit, and Windcut's fishers hold Taluma to evidence.

sections.heading: The constitution
paragraphs: At the winter hearings, Maro arranged small clay counters beside seven empty circles, one for each council seat. Esha asked the people to imagine one vacant.

Nemi wanted an interim official capable of keeping the drying racks, trading ground and fishing crews functioning. Seli wanted assurance that a caretaker would not become permanent simply by remaining long enough.

Dava proposed that the six remaining councillors could appoint a willing caretaker for no more than one moon cycle. The caretaker could coordinate ordinary services but could not declare war, sign a treaty, impose compulsory labor or claim new territory.

Any willing adult could be nominated by two resident households. Each adult, including elders, would have one confidential pebble choice, with voting hours accommodating work and care. A majority would elect the successor, with a runoff if necessary. Five independent residents chosen by lot could hear procedural appeals and order a new selection when rules were broken.
After two public readings, the constitution was ratified. Esha moved her pebble out of its circle for a moment. The circle remained.

sections.heading: The stores that were too full
paragraphs: Nemi faced a different problem: 314 settlement-days of food. It was an extraordinary achievement, but the stores were not one enormous, perfectly preserved supply. An old basket was opened. The upper layer was sound; its interior smelled wrong.
Eight settlement-days of spoiled or rejected food were recorded. Seli would not distribute doubtful food merely because the stores were full.

The council began rotating the oldest sound food first and inspecting stock before exchange. Six additional settlement-days went to voluntary nutrition, recovery and caregiving support. Twelve settlement-days were exchanged or gifted through limited, inspected contacts with willing neighbors. A provisional protected floor of 180 settlement-days was proposed, with existing family provisions and seed reserve untouched.
An apprentice stared at the remaining stores. "What do we do with all the rest?"
"Make sure it remains food," Nemi answered.

sections.heading: A borrowed frame and a tested knot
paragraphs: Ilan returned Renka's borrowed carrying frame through Oru and Tesh, along the permitted inland approach. At an invited upper-shelf meeting, Kelan demonstrated a textured protective wrapping. Four dry-load pulls performed well. In wet conditions, two of six trials slipped. No dangerous slope test was authorized.
Later, two Ridge Hearth adults attended a voluntary craft meeting in Taluma. No permanent road or treaty resulted.

At Windcut, Vara invited another controlled comparison. Four lashings were fitted to a removable host-owned frame, two conventional and two with Taluman sleeves. After rough tides one ordinary knot slipped and neither sleeved knot did, though one sleeve showed abrasion.
An apprentice called the design ready for export. "We have two tides," Vessa replied. "A season has more." No bulk production began.

stories.title: The Seats and the Stones
stories.deck: Taluma makes its founding principles binding and learns why an unmarked path can be an act of friendship.

sections.heading: A charter that outlives its authors
paragraphs: For the first time in Taluma's history, the Council of the Shore opened a hearing to decide rules that would outlive the people making them. The Hall of Many Hands filled twice, not once. At dawn, fishers returning from the tide flats spoke before sleeping. At dusk, people responsible for children and elders could attend while other adults covered their work.

Dava stood beside Maro's clay witness board and read the three principles the guiding intelligence had authorized. Any resident household could openly nominate a willing successor. No council seat could be inherited. And consequential decisions, including dissent, had to be recorded where people could hear them read back and challenge an inaccurate account.
Nemi placed his hand on the unfinished section of the board. "And when someone dies in the hungry part of winter, how long must we argue before the work is done?"
"We are deciding what the seat belongs to," Dava replied, "not who gets the next one."

The principles were ratified. Caretaker duration, the final selection threshold and appeals remained open for a separately witnessed charter amendment. Seven councillors remained in office. No apprentice gained a vote.

sections.heading: Renka's upper shelf
paragraphs: Inland, Ilan's party spent days arranging a meeting rather than cutting straight toward Windgrass Hollow. Oru and Tesh obtained consent from Ridge Hearth households for an escorted visit to a sheltered shelf chosen by Renka. Ilan brought Kelan and Leni, a sample of Taluman carrying-frame cordage, and no tools for quarrying or clearing a path.

Renka showed how a pebble marker could guide a welcome guest and also invite a stranger into another family's resting ground. Kelan demonstrated a replaceable fiber sleeve that protected a hauling knot from grit. A Ridge Hearth craftsperson answered by shifting the load point on a wooden frame.

A short downhill trial carried the weight more steadily. On damp grass, however, the revised hitch slipped and the load had to be caught before it struck a stone. They recorded both results. Nobody declared a new transport invention.

sections.heading: The sign that was not placed
paragraphs: A moon later, Renka and a willing companion came to Taluma, accompanied along accepted approaches by Oru and Tesh. They chose a public gathering at the Hall and could leave whenever they wished.

Vessa and Maren showed how sacrificial reed sleeves could be replaced without discarding an entire cord. Renka repeated the frame adjustment but declined to demonstrate certain trail signs away from her community.

When an apprentice proposed permanent stone markers between the communities, Renka overturned the proposed marker with her foot. Ilan suggested a removable sign placed only during a jointly agreed meeting and taken away afterward. Renka accepted it as a proposal, not continuing access.
Taluma learned that a stronger friendship sometimes required leaving a trail unmarked.

stories.title: The Weight of Seven Seats
stories.deck: The first succession charter, a cautious new horizon, and a knot that might one day carry Taluma's reputation.

sections.heading: The Hall of Many Hands
paragraphs: The Hall of Many Hands had hosted arguments over fish, timber, infants and trade. This time Esha asked the households to consider what would happen when the seven people sitting before them could no longer serve.

Dava had prepared a careful proposal: vacancies would be announced publicly, households could nominate willing adults, and the remaining council would appoint a temporary caretaker until the community chose a successor. The caretaker could keep water, food and repairs running but could not bind Taluma to war or a treaty. Each major council decision would carry the names of those who supported it and those who opposed it. No seat would pass from parent to child.
"Who gets to come here and nominate someone?" Seli asked. "A fisher who is out at the tide line? A mother keeping a sick child warm?"

Iset pointed out that a hearing attended only by those with spare hours would soon become rule by those with spare hours. Nemi feared the opposite danger: leaving a seat vacant too long while disputes multiplied. Maro marked the disagreement instead of erasing it.

The resulting Seven Seats charter was a complete draft, not law. Esha asked for another round of household testimony before the guiding intelligence decided whether to adopt it. The Listening Bench gained a real responsibility, but no votes or council seats.

sections.heading: Two tides at Windcut
paragraphs: Far south, Tidefin reached Windcut with Rela at the paddle and the revised bindings wrapped against salt. Vara met them outside the fishers' working stakes. Vessa and Maren had sent two comparably sized lashings and replaceable reed sleeves, each marked so a failed knot could be distinguished from a worn fiber. No one was asked to risk a loaded fish barrier.

When a rough tide passed, the ordinary cord had crept loose in the grit. The newly sleeved braid remained tied, but its outer fibers had begun to wear. The difference mattered, yet no one called the new design storm-proof.
Vara offered to compare further samples at two later seasonal visits, provided the fishers agreed again each time. Taluma returned with evidence, not a contract.

sections.heading: Beyond the old boundaries
paragraphs: Letha took Reedwing north with two other Taluman crew and Keshu, who volunteered as a Crescent pilot. The Ternhook households accepted one sheltered return stop. Beyond the already observed mouth of Northreach Estuary, Letha glimpsed a low dark ridge unfamiliar to her old chart. Farther in, something pale rose above the shore. Smoke, perhaps; spray or mist, just as plausibly.
Keshu pointed to a shoal cut where the tide was turning. Letha ordered the boat about. The ridge entered the atlas with a witness mark; the supposed smoke received a question mark.

Inland, Ilan returned to Upper Path to seek permission, not passage by assumption. Oru and Tesh consulted the seasonal Ridge Hearth households, who accepted a single escorted visit to an upper shoulder beyond the old Windgrass stopping place. There the path keeper Renka showed the visitors a loose-stone descent. They did not follow it. Instead she examined their carrying-frame lashings and suggested a future craft meeting at an agreed site.
There was no new road, quarry or treaty. There was, however, someone beyond the old frontier who might now recognize them when they returned.
